I built 2 AK's. It was a great learning experience and taught me a lot about how guns work. It really did not require the purchase of a lot of equipment. Everything seems hard when you haven't attempted it - then in hindsight you realize that it really wasn't. The heat treating and rivets were really very easy. I had a little bit of trouble improvising a means to bend the receiver, the first build required two attempts - the metal has to be clamped tightly in order to bend tightly along a reasonably sharp line. I found that the hardest part involved the head spacing, in part because I was trying to do my builds "on the cheep", and did not want to buy the appropriate gauges (my biggest mistake - just buy the gages and be done with it). The other thing that I found hard was making the replacement furniture. I used burled maple logs from my firewood pile relying upon a router, chisels, and sand paper. This took a lot of time but they both turned out very nice. The effort was well worth it.

Bending a receiver without a jig is so insane, I don't even want to argue the point. I just know that nothing good is going to come out if I were to attempt it. I am suitably impressed that you succeeded at it.

BTW, on an HK build there's not much choice about the headspacing. You just press the barrel into the truniuon until it stops. Of course, one checks the headspace at that point, but if the headspace fails, the only action to be taken is to scrap the build [*]. There's no way to press the barrel further in or pull it out and shim it. I still think it's a 100 times easier than the AK procedure.

[*] You can try to swap rollers out, but of course a parts kit comes without only 1 pair.
